title: Asset Library
subtitle: Market-proven logo and app-icon design styles. Every style comes with a breakdown of real commercial cases (where the look comes from and why it works) plus a copy-ready AI image prompt — drop in your brand name and go.

styles.name: Minimal Wordmark
styles.tagline: No icon, no tricks — the name is the logo
styles.intro: A text-only logo with no icon and no shape. The typeface is usually custom-built (Google's Product Sans, Uber's Uber Type), so the letterforms themselves are the brand asset. This is the default choice of the world's largest platforms: the simpler the mark, the easier it stays consistent across every size and every language.
why: Zero ambiguity: users read the brand name itself instead of decoding a shape first
Works at every scale: from a 16px favicon to a building sign, no redesign needed — a big advantage in app stores
Custom type is a moat: anyone can copy your name, nobody can copy your licensed letterforms
Cheap to localize: entering a new market means swapping text, not the visual system

cases.note: The 2015 colorful wordmark, set in custom Product Sans, still in use today.
The 2018 all-lowercase wordmark in custom Uber Type, identified purely by weight contrast.
Wordmark plus roundel in the modern system, Circular-derived type; the green is the brand.

styles.prompt: Design a logotype for {{BRAND_NAME}}: a clean geometric sans-serif wordmark, single solid color ({{COLOR}}), no icon, no gradient, no effects. Even letter spacing, neutral and friendly tone, must stay legible at 16px. Flat vector style on a pure white background.
styles.promptHint: Replace {{BRAND_NAME}} with your brand and {{COLOR}} with a hex value (e.g. #111827). Works with GPT-Image, Nano Banana, Gemini, and doubles as a design brief for a human designer.

styles.name: Negative Space
styles.tagline: Hide a shape between the letters — those who spot it remember you forever
styles.intro: Use the empty space between letters to form a hiddenshape as a bonus. The canonical example is the forward arrow living between the E and x in FedEx. Nothing is added to the design, yet it creates a moment of discovery — the second a viewer figures it out themselves, the memory sticks far harder than any explicit symbol.
why: Two readings: first the name, then the hidden shape — the second surprise is the shareable one
Restrained sophistication: theshape dissolves into the wordmark, keeping the mark minimal
Built-in social currency: 'did you notice the arrow in FedEx?' does the marketing for you
Best for established brands: it pays off only when viewers linger — risky for cold starts

cases.note: The gap between E and x forms a forward arrow — designed by Lindon Leader of Landor in 1994, the textbook negative-space case.
The arrow runs from a to z — everything under one roof — and doubles as a smile.

styles.prompt: Design a wordmark logo for {{BRAND_NAME}} that hides a subtle symbol in its negative space: the hidden shape should reference {{HIDDEN_MEANING, e.g. speed, growth, a location pin}} and appear only in the space between two letterforms. Single solid color {{COLOR}}, flat vector, white background, no shadows. The hidden shape must be formed by the negative space itself, never drawn as a separate icon.
styles.promptHint: Put one abstract concept (speed, growth, connection) in {{HIDDEN_MEANING}}. After generating, zoom in: the shape must be made of empty space, not a pasted-on icon — otherwise it isn't this style.

styles.name: Circular Badge
styles.tagline: A stamp-like circle that carries heritage and a quality promise
styles.intro: A centralshape inside a ring, brand name curved around it — like a certification stamp you could press onto a crate. Starbucks dropped even the outer text in 2011, leaving just the siren; BMW's roundel has kept its circular structure for a century. Badges age extremely well because they imply 'this brand has a past'.
why: Stamp psychology: circular badges read as certification, guarantee and lineage
Physical-friendly: lids, caps, embroidery, branding irons — any round surface takes it directly
Survives single color: shrink it, foil-stamp it, knock it out in white — it still works
Appreciates with age: badges accumulate trust over time, trend marks expire

cases.note: The 2011 siren roundel: brand name and outer text removed — pureshape confidence beyond words.
The blue-and-white quartered roundel — one of the most recognizable badges in motoring, unchanged in structure for a century.
A mountain-ridge badge with the name — outdoor fans call it 'the medal on your jacket'.

styles.prompt: Design a circular badge logo for {{BRAND_NAME}}: a ring-shaped emblem with {{CENTER_SUBJECT, e.g. a mountain ridge line, a wave, a rooster}} at the center, the brand name curved along the ring, maximum 2 colors ({{COLOR_1}}, {{COLOR_2}}), stamp-like flat style. It must stay readable at 24mm print size and work as a single-color white version. No photorealistic gradients.
styles.promptHint: Fill {{CENTER_SUBJECT}} with a concrete object tied to what the business does (mountains, waves, wheat). Always ask for a one-color version too — a badge's durability is decided by how it looks in single color.

styles.name: Combination Mark
styles.tagline: The icon carries memory, the wordmark carries the name
styles.intro: One abstract symbol paired with one wordmark, lockable side by side or split apart: the symbol for avatars and favicons, the wordmark for contracts and navigation. This has been the internet industry's default configuration for a decade — Slack's hashtag and Airbnb's Bélo both stood on their own as symbols first, then bound to the name.
why: Two memory channels: theshape handles 'I've seen this', the text handles 'what it's called' — highest recall
Scene-adaptive: symbol for narrow containers (app icons), full lockup for formal contexts
Symbol-first spread: in feeds, the shape gets recognized faster than wordmarks
Caveat: young brands should not go symbol-only — before users know your name, a shape is a dead asset
fits: Companies with many touchpoints (web / apps / documents)

cases.note: The four-color hashtag comes from the idea of channels; symbol and wordmark work fully independently.
The Bélo plus wordmark lockup: one symbol for people, places, love and belonging — launched in 2014 with a full usage guide.
The 1977 rainbow apple: the early proof that a symbol can stand alone without the name.

styles.prompt: Create a combination logo for {{BRAND_NAME}}: a simple abstract symbol based on {{SYMBOL_CONCEPT, e.g. a hashtag for chat channels, a nested chevron for layers}} paired with a horizontal wordmark in a modern grotesque font. The symbol must work alone as an app icon; the wordmark must work alone in documents. 2-4 flat colors, generous clear space, white background, vector style.
styles.promptHint: Give {{SYMBOL_CONCEPT}} an abstract idea tied to the product so the symbol has a reason to exist. Test the output twice: symbol alone — recognizable? Wordmark alone — readable?

styles.name: Geometric Gradient
styles.tagline: Shapes plus tech-color gradients: instantly reads as 'product company'
styles.intro: Basic geometric primitives (rounded rectangles, circles) assembled into a letter or abstract mark, with 2-5 saturated brand colors or a gradient. Stripe, Figma and Discord defined the SaaS-era aesthetic with this language: the palette itself is the design system's spec sheet.
why: Color as asset: Figma's five colors, Discord's blurple — hex codes become brand property
Dark-UI native: gradients glow on dark backgrounds, a perfect fit for developer tools
Extensible: the geometric units recombine into illustrations, icons and loading animations
Risk: trend-heavy — dozens of lookalike product marks shipped around 2016; keep shape differentiation sharp

cases.note: The purple slashed-S plus wordmark — 'Stripe purple' became the payment industry's default association.
Five rounded geometric blocks form the F; each color maps to a canvas concept — the color system is the product philosophy.
The 2021 wordmark plus gamepad-face symbol, with blurple running through every touchpoint.

styles.prompt: Design a geometric logo mark for {{BRAND_NAME}} built from {{N}} simple shapes (circles and rounded rectangles) that reads as an abstract {{LETTER_OR_OBJECT, e.g. the letter S, a spark}}. Use a subtle two-tone gradient from {{COLOR_A}} to {{COLOR_B}}, plus a neutral sans wordmark. Must look right on both dark and light backgrounds. Flat vector, no bevels or 3D effects.
styles.promptHint: Setting {{LETTER_OR_OBJECT}} to the brand's initial letter works best for geometric assembly. Ask the model to render it on both dark and light backgrounds before choosing.

styles.name: Mascot Character
styles.tagline: Turn the brand into a character with a personality, not just a mark
styles.intro: The brand becomes a drawable character: Duolingo's owl Duo runs the company's social media with 'threatening-you-into-studying' gags, and Michelin's Bibendum has been standing since 1898. Of all logo structures, the mascot is the only one that can make faces — born for content distribution.
why: Emotional asset: a character has expressions and moods, producing content instead of just displaying a logo
Trust shortcut: in education and service, a likeable character collapses psychological distance
Merch and IP-ready: stickers, plush toys, collaborations — characters commercialize naturally
Maintenance cost: characters need ongoing operation (persona, illustration guidelines); stop and they age
fits: Consumer brands running heavy social media

cases.note: Owl Duo: the mascot became the social-media lead character — the persona itself is a growth strategy.
Bibendum, born 1898 — a figure made of stacked tires, among the longest-lived mascots in commercial history.

styles.prompt: Draw a friendly mascot logo for {{BRAND_NAME}}: a single cartoon character ({{ANIMAL_OR_PERSON, e.g. an owl, a chef}}) with bold outlines, 2-3 flat colors, expressive eyes conveying {{TRAIT, e.g. playful persistence}}, simple enough to be embroidered or made into a sticker. Optional brand name curved below. No shading, no fur detail, flat vector style.
styles.promptHint: Put a personality trait users should feel into {{TRAIT}}. Shrink the result to 32px: a mascot that turns to mush won't survive as an app icon.

styles.name: Luxury Serif
styles.tagline: Black and white, hairline serifs, wide space — restraint is the price tag
styles.intro: High-contrast Didone serifs (Didot / Bodoni family), pure black and white, zero ornament. Tiffany and Vogue wordmarks and Rolex's crown have barely changed in decades. The language borrows from classical print and haute-couture typography: by chasing no trend, it becomes the anti-trend.
why: Class association: hairline serifs automatically evoke fashion magazines, bespoke ateliers and classic taste
Never expires: precisely because it rides no contemporary trend, it needs no rebrand
Print-friendly: single color suffices — blind emboss, foil, embroidery all compatible
Hard constraint: on mass-market budget products it reads as pretentious — typeface temperament must match price point

cases.note: A high-contrast serif wordmark in the same classical lineage as Vogue: the blue box carries the color, the letterforms carry the restraint.
A Didot-family high-contrast wordmark — the typographic archetype of all fashion publishing.
Crown plus all-caps serif wordmark: recognition carried entirely by letterform and proportion, no decoration.

styles.prompt: Create a luxury wordmark for {{BRAND_NAME}} in a high-contrast Didone serif (thin hairlines, strong stems), all capitals, wide letter spacing, pure black on white. Optionally add an interlocked monogram of the initials {{INITIALS}}. No gradients, no ornaments, no gold: the premium feel must come from typographic restraint alone.
styles.promptHint: Image models love to 'add ornament' whenever they hear serif — the prompt already forbids it; still check the output for stray flourish strokes.

styles.name: Terminal / Dev-Native
styles.tagline: A tiny black-and-white glyph with monospace energy: 'built for developers'
styles.intro: One minimal geometric glyph (Vercel's triangle) plus a lowercase sans wordmark, in pure black and white or a single accent color (Supabase green). The aesthetic descends from terminals and ASCII culture: the anti-marketing posture is itself a filter — developers see 'not flashy' and conclude 'this team gets engineering'.
why: In-group signal: stark black and white is developer culture's handshake, implying the product respects the craft
Survives tiny sizes: favicons, terminals, README badges — exactly its core distribution surfaces
Dark-mode native: the product UI is dark anyway, so the logo inverts to white and just works
Risk: hard to break out — to mainstream consumers it can read as cold

cases.note: A single black equilateral triangle: among the stingiest — and most self-consistent — glyphs in logo history.
A hairline wordmark on dark ground — 'Linear aesthetics' became shorthand for product polish.
A green lightning glyph — the signature color of the open-source database world, single-color by design.

styles.prompt: Design a developer-brand logo for {{BRAND_NAME}}: a single geometric glyph ({{SHAPE, e.g. an upward triangle, a terminal cursor block}}) in pure black or one accent color ({{ACCENT}}) on a plain background, plus a lowercase sans wordmark with a monospace feel. It must render cleanly at 16px favicon size and invert to white for dark mode. Flat, no gradients, no effects.
styles.promptHint: Ask for both white-on-black and black-on-white versions — half the value of a terminal-style logo is its inverted form.

styles.name: Solid Glyph
styles.tagline: One flat color, one symbol — still readable at 16px
styles.intro: A single background color and one high-contrast symbol: no gradients, no text. This is the most noise-proof move in an icon ocean — among dozens of App Store icons, a solid block plus a simple shape is read in 0.1 seconds. Spotify green, Things orange, Claude cream: the color itself is the entry point.
why: Color asset: keep one exclusive hue and users find you by scanning
Never smudges at tiny sizes: few strokes means notification bar, watch and dark mode all work
Merch-friendly: a clean color block on any backdrop, zero-cost marketing art
Constraint: the hue must be near-exclusive — a color clash means sharing traffic

cases.note: Black sound-wave arcs on green; only the stroke weight has ever been tweaked, and the 'green = music' grip has never been taken.
One white arrow on orange — a paid productivity tool dares to use a toy-bright color because the glyph is absolutely simple.
An orange starburst on cream: while every AI product went dark, the warm hand-drawn feel became the identifier.

styles.prompt: Design an app icon for {{APP_NAME}}: one flat solid background ({{COLOR_1}}), one high-contrast centered glyph ({{COLOR_2}}), no gradients, no text, no shadows. The glyph must stay legible at 29x29 px. Rounded-square iOS icon format, 1024x1024, generous padding, flat vector style.
styles.promptHint: Pick a {{COLOR_1}} you can own long-term and max out the contrast with {{COLOR_2}}; shrink to 29px and check it still reads.

styles.name: Gradient
styles.tagline: The gradient 'premium feel' is the most validated recipe there is
styles.intro: A colorful gradient base plus a white line glyph — since Instagram this has all but become the uniform of consumer breakout apps. The gradient gives a static icon light and depth while the white foreground keeps the glyph clean. Only To-C products dare saturated gradients — the signal is 'popular, energetic, worth opening'.
why: Free premium: one gradient replaces a whole skeuomorphic highlight stack — the icon instantly costs more
White foreground is lazy-proof: the glyph never has to blend with the base
Works on light and dark wallpapers: gradients carry their own light
Constraint: hue real estate is crowded — avoid the ranges Instagram / Apple Music already own

cases.note: Swapped the skeuomorphic camera for a pink-orange-yellow gradient and within months 'candy' became its unofficial nickname.
A blue-violet gradient sparkle — Google unified its entire AI line under this breathing light effect.
A white note on pink gradient: the most 'neon' tile in Apple's own grid, aimed straight at young music scenes.
A paper plane on blue-cyan gradient, camped opposite WhatsApp green; the gradient gives the plane volume.

styles.prompt: Design an app icon for {{APP_NAME}}: a smooth diagonal gradient background ({{COLOR_1}} to {{COLOR_2}}, optional third hue), a single white outline glyph of {{SUBJECT}} centered, no text, soft light sheen, rounded-square iOS icon format, 1024x1024, flat modern style like a top-charting consumer app.
styles.promptHint: Check your gradient hues aren't already Instagram / Apple Music / Telegram territory; keep the white glyph under three main curves.

styles.name: Lettermark
styles.tagline: One letter fills the screen — even a rename can't dislodge it
styles.intro: Turn the brand's initial into the only graphic: Uber's U, X's X, Netflix's N. The lettermark is the privilege of category-defining platforms — users already know the word, so the icon just repeats it. The letter fills the canvas with almost no ornament: the most confident posture in any list.
why: Zero learning cost: icon and name are the same thing — remembering one remembers the other
Rename-proof: Twitter → X changed only the letter and the whole visual system survived
Composition is inherently stable: one big centered character never smudges
Constraint: for a startup, a lettermark just magnifies a name nobody knows

cases.note: A white U on black, distilled from a busy map glyph to a single letter — the act of restraint was itself the confidence statement.
The Twitter bird retired and the letter X took everything — the largest-ever 'rename without moving the visual center' experiment.
The gradient Bélo on white: one mark that is simultaneously the letter A, a heart, a person and a location pin.
A folded red N on black, film-strip depth built into the strokes — the brand color is the channel color.

styles.prompt: Design an app icon for {{APP_NAME}}: a single bold letter "{{LETTER}}" filling the canvas, custom geometric sans-serif, {{COLOR_1}} background with {{COLOR_2}} letter (or inverted), no extra ornament, the letter may carry one subtle fold or gradient detail, rounded-square iOS icon format, 1024x1024.
styles.promptHint: The letter should span at least 60% of the width to 'fill the screen'; at most one decorative detail, and it must vanish cleanly at 29px.

styles.name: Mascot
styles.tagline: Put the character's face on the icon — the bond forms before the app even opens
styles.intro: A mascot icon fits an expressive character into 1024px: Duolingo's owl, Reddit's Snoo, bilibili's little TV. Characters carry personality and fan-art space; users open the app 'to see what it's doing today' — the favorite weapon of retention-obsessed categories (learning, community, youth culture).
why: Emotional entry: costumes swap with holidays and events — the icon itself becomes content
Memory beats geometry: humans remember faces far better than shapes, it pops out of any list
Social amplifier: sticker packs, merch, animation — the icon is just the starting point
Constraint: once a character lands it's nearly impossible to replace; budget for the IP early

cases.note: Duo the owl permanently headlines the 'scariest study nag' meme — the icon is the marketing, at half budget.
Snoo, the antenna-topped white figure on orange: the whole community vibe rests on that harmless face, barely redrawn for years.
A pink little TV — chassis plus two antennae say 'ACG community' completely.

styles.prompt: Design an app icon for {{APP_NAME}}: a friendly {{CREATURE}} mascot face centered on a {{COLOR_1}} background, big eyes, simple rounded shapes, flat illustration style with soft shading, no text, must stay readable at 29x29 px, rounded-square iOS icon format, 1024x1024.
styles.promptHint: Head only, no full body; bind {{CREATURE}} to the product's temperament (learning = owl, community = little robot) and give the eyes at least a third of the face width.

styles.name: Rich Texture
styles.tagline: A stroke of paint, a sliver of light — an icon built like a small artwork
styles.intro: Real light, paint and material turn the icon into a miniature artwork: Procreate's rainbow brush stroke, Genshin's metal crest. The textured route keeps getting validated in the two experience-heavy categories — creative tools and games: the more the icon looks like a poster, the more users trust the product's quality.
why: Quality signal: brushwork and lighting declare 'this is for people who do serious work'
Instant standout: most of the list is flat color blocks, one textured icon jumps out
Emotional density: games pre-stage their world, tools pay homage to craft
Constraint: detail dies at small sizes — ship a simplified variant for notification bars

cases.note: One wet rainbow stroke on black — the 'sharpen your tools' manifesto compressed into a single brush mark.
A platinum-gradient metal crest: the game's Teyvat worldview rendered as a collectible badge.

styles.prompt: Design an app icon for {{APP_NAME}}: a single dramatic {{TEXTURE_SUBJECT}} (brush stroke / emblem / artifact) with realistic lighting and rich color on a dark {{COLOR_1}} background, poster-quality rendering, centered composition, no text, rounded-square iOS icon format, 1024x1024.
styles.promptHint: Render two versions: the 1024 detail cut and a 29px simplified cut; keep exactly one textured subject — cut the second element.

styles.name: Colorful Geometric
styles.tagline: Three or four colors assembled into one shape — the professional tool uniform
styles.intro: Several saturated blocks assembled into a single mark: Figma's four-color bars, Slack's colored hash, Google Photos' four-color pinwheel. Multicolor geometry is the safest language for collaboration and productivity tools — each color can map to a product module, making the icon a legend for the information architecture.
why: Color as function: icon palette maps one-to-one to the in-app palette, closing the recognition loop
Breaks the serious-tool monotony: professional apps can't be cutesy, but they can be multicolor
Structure that splits: one mark of interlocking parts feeds motion, loaders and brand kits alike
Constraint: hold the palette to 3-5 colors — beyond that it's a paint aisle

cases.note: Four colored rounded bars assemble an outline — the colors of the product panels are the colors of the icon.
A colored hash: the abstract idea of 'channel' drawn directly as four arcs.
A four-color pinwheel — 'photos auto-arranged into albums' rotated into a single shape.

styles.prompt: Design an app icon for {{APP_NAME}}: one unified mark assembled from 3-4 rounded geometric shapes, each in a distinct saturated color ({{COLOR_1}}, {{COLOR_2}}, {{COLOR_3}}, optional {{COLOR_4}}), on a white or very light background, flat vector, precise alignment, no text, rounded-square iOS icon format, 1024x1024.
styles.promptHint: Fix 3-4 HEX values before writing the prompt; the shapes must overlap or interlock — laid out separately they become a swatch strip.

styles.name: Minimal Light
styles.tagline: One blank amid a screen of color steals the show
styles.intro: White background plus a single thin dark glyph — trading away color presence for 'premium and calm': Notion's serifed N, Threads' tangled line. In an ocean of colorful icons, white is contrarianly loud; it also promises the product UI is just as clean — the icon is the trailer for the product's temperament.
why: Contrarian placement: a white block pops hardest on dark wallpapers and turns 'papery' on light ones
Temperament trailer: white plus hairline = restrained, professional, document-like — expectation management for free
Never dates: black on white carries no trend-color risk, no redraw for a decade
Constraint: the glyph must be distinctive, or white-on-black reads as a built-in system app
fits: Professional products after a composed feel

cases.note: A black serifed N on white — one letter that borrows the entire 'paper and pen' tradition.
A single tangled curve on white: Meta's way of drawing a line from Instagram's rainbow gradient.

styles.prompt: Design an app icon for {{APP_NAME}}: pure white background, one thin elegant {{COLOR_1}} glyph of {{SUBJECT}} (single continuous line preferred), generous negative space, editorial minimal style, no gradients, no text, rounded-square iOS icon format, 1024x1024.
styles.promptHint: Keep stroke weight above 1/40 of the canvas width or it breaks at small sizes; if the glyph is generic, add one proprietary detail (like Notion's serif foot).

styles.name: Dark Tech
styles.tagline: A cold gleam on black — engineers spot their own at a glance
styles.intro: Near-black base plus a high-contrast glyph or subtle glow: Linear, Obsidian, ChatGPT. The dark icon broke out of developer tools and is now the default skin of 'AI-native' — it assumes the user keeps dark mode on all day, and the icon is one cold gleam in the dark ocean.
why: Native to dark mode: developers and AI users live in dark UIs — no inversion needed
Cold filter: black carries a 'capabilities, not marketing' air that screens out non-target users
Glow memory: one gradient gleam is the entire decoration — restraint is the identifier
Constraint: risky for mass consumer apps — black triggers 'professional software anxiety'

cases.note: Concentric colored arcs on near-black — 'Linear aesthetics' has become the name of a design school.
A glowing crystal on deep purple: the knowledge tool carves the 'mined ore' metaphor right into the icon.
A white knot-flower on black — the most imitated silhouette of the AI era.

styles.prompt: Design an app icon for {{APP_NAME}}: near-black background (#0B0B0F), a single minimal glyph of {{SUBJECT}} in white or a subtle {{COLOR_1}} glow gradient, thin precise strokes, dark-mode native, no text, no drop shadow, rounded-square iOS icon format, 1024x1024.
styles.promptHint: One glow color, one direction only; also export a pure-white inverted variant for light contexts.
